source.title: Exploring Sparse Autoencoders in Text-Based Causal Confounding Adjustment
source.authors: Mian Zhong; Katherine A. Keith; Anjalie Field

record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse autoencoders as representations for a causal-adjustment pipeline, but its results concern causal-estimation performance and diagnostics, not whether superposition occurs or what geometry SAE features have.
record.gate_note: The SAEs are trained on pretrained text embeddings, not analyzed as LLM activation features. The paper reports an SAE sparsity ablation and feature-selection diagnostics; these are recorded as findings about SAE settings, not as evidence for any listed claim version. Main adjustment comparisons and cited claims about SAEs do not measure superposition, neuron polysemanticity, or feature geometry.
record.test_reason: The study uses top-K SAEs trained on pretrained text embeddings (not LLM activations) as covariates for causal adjustment. Its results are bias, RMSE, coverage, ESS, SMD and feature-selection counts for causal estimation. None of these measures superposition, polysemanticity, feature geometry, or whether SAE features are canonical units of a model.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. SAE-based representations give lower bias and higher coverage in the binary and multi-class 20NG settings. Multi-label EURLEX results are mixed: CEM has low bias but under 1% of treated units retained, and DoubleML bias stays high. Interpretable features support falsification diagnostics. No claims about superposition are made.
record.recipe_differences: Uses top-K SAEs trained on pretrained text embeddings, followed by feature selection and causal estimators; it does not apply or reproduce a superposition measurement or intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that changing SAE sparsity K affects causal-estimation metrics, and that changing representation dimension M affects how many features are selected.

fits_no_version.finding: In the EURLEX multi-label setting (SAEselect+CEM, M=128), causal bias and RMSE vary with SAE sparsity K. The authors say greater sparsity generally improves RMSE and data retention, while coverage improves with less sparsity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE sparsity settings trade off downstream causal-adjustment metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: At M=128, the multi-class and multi-label settings select more SAE features (medians above 40 of 128). At M=32, nearly all features are selected in those settings; the authors read this as M=32 being insufficiently expressive.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The number of SAE features needed for an adjustment task depends on dictionary size and confounder complexity.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The relevant results are indirect: they evaluate downstream causal adjustment rather than superposition or feature geometry. The experiments are semi-synthetic and depend on selected datasets, confounder definitions, and hyperparameters; the authors note that results may vary under other settings.
record.rows_left_out: Main comparisons of causal-estimation pipelines, matching diagnostics, and alternative CEM cut-point results were left out because they do not measure the claim's representational features or geometry. Values visible only in Fig. 4 for coverage and treated retention were also omitted; the text gives only qualitative trends for those metrics.

untested.parts: No toy models; no test of overlapping or nearly orthogonal directions, a sparsity-dependent transition, or geometry.
No analysis of neuron polysemanticity or capacity competition.
No analysis of the causes of polysemanticity.
SAEs are trained on OpenAI text-embedding outputs used as data representations. No LLM activation features or neuron-distribution analysis.
No test of the completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features as a model's units. Feature-selection variance across seeds concerns the Lasso selection step, not SAE stability.
No test of one-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Every row is a performance or diagnostic number for the study's own pipeline, so no verdicts apply. The authors cite SAE work describing features as atomic and interpretable, but they do not test this. Their remark that religion features may be encoded 'less atomically' is a speculative interpretation of selection variance, not a measurement.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test overlapping, nearly orthogonal feature directions, a sparsity-dependent superposition transition, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not investigate causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity occurs without capacity pressure.
Does not examine feature distributions across LLM neurons or recover features from LLM activations; its SAE input is pretrained text embeddings.
Does not test SAE-feature completeness, stability, or canonical status as units of a model's representation.
Does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.
